utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today, Wednesday, the 30th of August, I'd like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel. I see that Mr. Karnavas isn't present. I would also like to greet the accused. And in particular, I would like to greet our new registrar, who is replacing Mr. Frejabue. On behalf of all the Judges I would like to welcome him, and I'm absolutely persuaded that he will facilitate the work for all of us. Today we will be continuing with the cross-examination of a witness, but first of all there are a number of things I would like to deal with. According to the calculations made by the registrar, Mr. Praljak's Defence has another 64 minutes. Mr. Petkovic's Defence has 45 minutes and Mr. Coric's defence has 45 minutes. If no one takes up more time than allocated to them, it should be possible for us to conclude the examination of this witness today. And the second point I wanted to mention is, although Mr. Karnavas isn't here, yesterday he took the floor, made some submissions. The Judges discussed the matter, but I must admit that we failed to understand what his purpose was. When he is present we will give him the floor again so he can explain himself again. And then the third point. Next week with regard to witness -- or with regard to the Prosecution's expert witness, the Judges discussed this problem yesterday afternoon and we have reached a decision. We will allow the Prosecution to have two complete days. We know they wanted nine hours. Two days, that amounts to eight hours, so we would like the Prosecution to limit themselves to these two days. In light of our previous decisions, we have decided to grant the Defence a total of three days. It is up to the Defence to reach an agreement and to see how they will share this time amongst themselves. If Mr. Prlic's counsel wants to take up all the time because all the other Defence teams grant him their time, that's up to the Defence. Otherwise, we will have to rule. But we hope that all members of the Defence will be in a position to reach a decision with regard to who should take up a certain amount of time in the cross-examination. The witness's report, the expert witness's report is structured on the basis of a plan, and the Prosecution should follow this plan when examining the witness, because the report contains footnotes that refer to various documents, various publications such as official bulletins, Official Gazettes, et cetera. Some of these documents have already been mentioned or referred to so that when questions are put the witness -- when we decide on the admission of certain documents after the witness's testimony we can move on very quickly. We can say such-and-such a decree is concerned of such-and-such a date, et cetera. I believe Defence counsel should discuss the way in which they would like to divide the time amongst themselves, since last time Mr. Prlic intervened and said that his name appeared on a number of occasions very frequently in the expert's report, and he, therefore, believed that he should have a sufficient amount of time to cross-examine the witness or, rather, for his counsel to cross-examine the witness. However, if you fail to reach an agreement -- if the Defence fails to reach an agreement, the Chamber will have to rule and decide on the amount of time to be allocated to each member of the Defence team. Next week we will be rendering decisions concerning 94 bis. This was requested by the Prosecution. We will soon be completing that decision, and you will have it next week. There are also two decisions that concern 92 bis, and these decisions will likewise be rendered in the near future. So we are not late. We are trying to render these decisions as quickly as possible. We know that nature abhors a vacuum so that as soon as one decision is rendered you are ready to file a motion for another decision. Mr. Scott, you have the floor. I see that you have a map there that may be useful for all the parties involved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. The map, I think, is for Mr. Praljak's use and we will see how that goes. I just wanted to respond very, very quickly to the witness next week. As the Chamber has cut our time, the Prosecution's proposed time a bit, and again indicated we should move of course as efficiently as possible, it would help us and assist us in doing so, Your Honour, if we could clarify that the -- the expert could make more frequent use or reference to his report. It seems to us again that when everyone in the courtroom had the report and Your Honour had the report and had a chance to study the report before the witness comes, that it is most efficient if the Prosecutor can take the witness through the report, highlight those most important points, to make the witness available for cross-examination, of course, and for clarifying questions from the Judges, but to -- actually you had the report in front of everyone and to work essentially off the basis of the report. If the Chamber will allow us to do that, I think we can indeed take the witness more efficiently and may even be able to improve on the two full days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before I give the floor to Mr. Murphy, Mr. Scott, I assume when the hearing of the expert witnesses has been completed you will be requesting that the report be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask the court to bear in mind when the Prosecution conducts the case in that way, what they do is essentially add to the examination-in-chief of the witness a long and detailed document, in this case well over a hundred pages if my recollection is correct, containing references to many hundreds of documents. It's also a document, Your Honour, which I think refers individually to each of the accused, and what the Court is doing, and this happened in the case of Mr. Beese to some extent also, is to essentially give the Prosecution an extra couple of days of examination-in-chief in written form. It would, of course, take them many days to elicit all of the information in that report by means of examination-in-chief. So if the Prosecution is to be permitted to do that, Your Honour, and to admit that document in evidence, then I would submit that the Defence should be entitled to ample time to challenge not only the testimony but also the detail of that report including the many documents and footnotes referred to. And, Your Honour, we have already had a meeting of Defence counsel to discuss this situation. We hope to reach a large area of agreement as to the conduct of the cross-examination, and we think we can do that successfully. But I do ask the Court to bear in mind that if Mr. Scott does follow that strategy, we may at some point need to ask the Court for some indulgence in order to conduct a fair and efficient cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can have one more minute. With all respect to my learned friend, I think that turns the whole process on its head. The entire reason that Rule 94 bis requires that a report be provided -- prepared unlike other usual witnesses, this is so that everyone will have the report in the courtroom ahead of time. This is not a factual witness and a victim witness in the usual sense, and there is no reason -- the Prosecution submits there is no reason not to gain the efficiency of using the report in the courtroom. A report is prepared under the rules and then we turn around and act like, we pretend that the report doesn't exist even though everyone has it, everyone has had it for months, and then we proceed in a very cumbersome and slow way to do business. Of course, of course the Defence will have a chance to cross-examine on the entire report. That's why they've had it for the last three months. So there's no -- there's no -- there's no dispute about that. So I don't accept or excuse me I respectfully disagree with Mr. Murphy's point and we'll proceed -- and, of course, they have more time than we have. Our time has been cut; their time has been increased. And all I'm saying is that in order that we can do it more efficiently, if we can make more direct use of the report it will be more efficient for everyone, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, as a general rule, and this is how things have functioned here at the Tribunal to date, when there is an expert report, the Prosecution or the Defence provide the other party with the report so that they can examine it, and at that point in time they request that the report be admitted into evidence. Sometimes the Prosecution is happy with just having the report and it's just a cross-examination. When there's something contested, the report is not admitted, and the Prosecution then has to conduct its examination-in-chief. So this is the hypothesis we're dealing with. They then need time. And on that basis the Defence cross-examines the witnesses. We function within a system in which the parties obtain witnesses for the Chamber, but in the continental system the Chamber assigns an expert. This system, the procedure we follow here is that the Prosecution presents its expert who is cross-examined or examined and then the Defence can also ask for its expert appear, can say contradictory things, and then that expert is also cross-examined. So there is a balance. This expert will be discussing the HVO structure. The Prosecution will have questions for the witness as well as the Judges. You will then cross-examine this expert, and if you want to add any additional information to what's said on the HVO structure you will call your own expert who will contradict the testimony of the first expert. So as you can see, no prejudice is caused to you. But obviously when you call your own witness to discuss the HVO structure, at that point in time you will have a sufficient amount of time and the Prosecution will have less time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I don't disagree at all with that, and we have absolutely no objection -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I have no objection, of course, to the Prosecution taking all the time they want in introducing this evidence. The only point I make is this: As the Court is aware, this expert is an employee of the Prosecution. He is going to effectively present their entire case in -- in -- really in a narrative form, and for us to have the opportunity to fulfil our obligations under Rule 90, to put our case fully to the witness, and I think this was actually the point that Mr. Karnavas was making to Your Honours yesterday, that we have that obligation. For us to do that, Your Honour, it takes a certain time, and my only point is we should be given time to do that in an appropriate way so that the Court can understand the Defence case on this point. That's the only point that I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic, please be very brief, because time is limited. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll be very brief. Naturally I reject the suggestion made by the Prosecution. I won't comment on your decision. It is such as it is. You probably have your own reasons for it. But it's for you to decide how you will treat this expert we'll be hearing next week. When we have a criteria I believe we must respect it completely. Yesterday you mentioned a word, "precision." This is a very important word. Niels Bohr, an eminent physicist, was discussing the meaning of "Wahrheit" or truth. He said it should be "Klarheit," clarity, so truth must be equivalent to precision. So far the Prosecution has had the same amount of time, eight or nine hours that's not much of a difference here. The OTP has been dealing with such matters for over seven years. They know how they'll deal with this work, whether they'll be granted eight or nine hours it's not much of a difference. Regardless of my request, the time for Defence is the same. And now we're trying to reduce the time allocated to the Defence so that it's not even necessary to do what is necessary in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In examination-in-chief, correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this historian of the 19th century should be granted a sufficient amount of time to present all of his arguments before the Chamber and the public so that we from the Defence can put relevant questions to him. Certain rules are treated in an absurd manner. For example, the discussion could have proceeded in the following way: Mr. Scott could have said, I have no questions because the report is quite clear. Mr. Tomljanovich, is there anything you would like to say or add. And he'll say no. Everything is in the report. This would have taken up 24 seconds if we divided that by six, according to that rule, I'd have four seconds for my cross-examination. So it's necessary to demonstrate flexibility and to base oneself on the merits so all the rules have sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the position of the Chamber has been very clearly explained by our Presiding Judge, President Antonetti, I don't want to prolong this debate but simply to add that then the Chamber has made this decision. It has, of course, departed from the rule which had been previously established and which was also confirmed by the Appeals Chamber, and that is that roughly the time is -- usually is being divided between the two parties 50/50 per cent. Now when we have allotted two days for the Prosecution and three days to the Defence, it is a departure from this rule, which means that the -- anyway, the Defence will have about 50 per cent more time than the Prosecution has, and really we believe that it is a fair treatment of the rights of the Defence for a fair trial and, therefore, I believe that it should be taken into account hopefully it will be followed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll now move on. Everyone has expressed their point of view. I do agree with Mr. Prlic as far as precision is concerned. The Judges, when putting their questions, always trying to obtain precise testimony. Justice must be precise and approximations must be avoided and sometimes we need time to be precise. We are fully aware of this fact. We'll now continue. Mr. Praljak, as I've already said, you have 64 minutes left. Please go ahead. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I'm going to start straight away, and I should like to ask the usher to place on the ELMO Exhibit 3D 00365. It is a report. It's an article appearing in the Independent, actually, written by a journalist who entered on the 21st of August, 1993, with the convoy. And it's a very short text. The Independent paper's journalist claims that when the convoy entered -- when the convoy entered that the BH army soldiers from the surrounding buildings shot with snipers and tried to trigger off a reaction from the HVO, because when the convoy entered, there was supposed to be a cease-fire, a truce, no shooting. So in that way they wanted to provoke a reaction from the HVO for them to return fire and perhaps hit some of you, your men, the escorts of the convoy, or perhaps civilians, to cause civilian casualties. And he was -- an officer of the UN was warned of this. And in the film that we saw, the footage presented by the Prosecution, we saw a BH army soldier using an RPG to shoot. We saw him shooting, I don't suppose at his own building or his own people. So, sir, could you tell me now, please, whether you, while you were on the spot on that occasion, did you see at that same situation as described by the lady journalist in the text that I have indicated here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you speaking about the first convoy that went into Mostar or was it the second one with the 60 tonnes? Which of the two convoys are you referring to? Would you mind clarifying that, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. No, the second convoy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second convoy, that's the one I was with. It was not shot at, at all, at any time while you were going into east Mostar. There was no firing. Now, I haven't read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that the 28th of August, I think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Because the article we have on our screens is dated the 28th of August. So if there was an event that took place on the 28th of August, the Independent had time to write the article and print it the same day? Is that what you're saying, Mr. Praljak? Was it the convoy of the 21st or the 28th? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I think that the journalist of the Independent was not able to send off his text the same day, so I assume that this was on the 25th. So the convoy was on the 25th. And we had this article published in the papers three days later, and that would be a reasonable time during which to expect a journalist to do his duty and write his report and send it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I must insist on the fact that even though I haven't really become totally familiar with the contents of this article, if this is the convoy that I accompanied, and I think the picture is of that convoy, well, there were no -- there was no firing at all on that convoy. Now, as to the previous convoy, I don't know. I wasn't there. I don't know. I don't think there was any shooting because otherwise I would know. I would have known about it. But I don't think there was any shooting at that convoy either. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. There was no shooting on the part of the HVO. Here it is claimed that the sniper shots came from the BH army side shooting at the HVO side in order to provoke a response from the HVO. And on the footage that we saw from the Prosecutor, we see a BH army soldier with his RPG rifle shooting at the opposite side trying to provoke it so that the HVO could respond. So what I'm asking you is, did you see this same thing that the journalist described? Did you notice snipers on the BH army side shooting at the opposite side, and did you see this activity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you answer, just a moment, please. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, two things. First of all, I think it would be helpful if the Chamber could see the -- actually be able to read the article. I don't know if the Chamber has the facility to enlarge it or not. In the form that it's presently being displayed I'm not sure anyone can actually read it except for the headlines and the largest print. I think if Mr. Praljak is going to use a document everyone in the courtroom should be able to see exactly what the document says or doesn't say and put it in context. I don't think there's anything in the article -- some of the things that Mr. Praljak has said are not completely a fair characterisation of the article, number one. Number two, I think it's a mischaracterisation of the evidence to say that the photograph of the soldier with the rocket-propelled grenade launcher, the RPG, is necessarily in the footage connected to anything that happened on the 28th of -- there was -- 28th of August, 1993. As other people have said, parts of the film are obviously a compilation of footage. There is no indication that Mr. Praljak's representation is true, that that particular event actually happened on or around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to take note of what you said. Now, you were asked a question, Witness. Would you answer that question now, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At no time while I was with the convoy going into east Mostar was I the witness of any firing or any snipers or saw the BH army using snipers to provoke any type of reaction at all. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you move this article to the right, please, because -- no. Other side. I made an exact mark of a portion that can be read. I have singled it out, so that's what I was referring to. But we've dealt with that article. It's quite clearly stated here. And I'd like to tender this into evidence. I should now like to ask Your Honour to tell me or, rather, I'd like to ask the witness some facts from document P 5111. They are SpaBat reports, and I'm asking whether this is a protected document, whether it's under seal. Do we need to go into closed session, private session, or can I ask the witness quite openly about it in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's under seal is it? Yes, it's under seal. Let's move into private session then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, now that we are back in open session, perhaps you could put that question to the witness again if you think it's important. The question that concerned someone else who had the same family name as you do. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of another man with the last name of Praljak within the HVO structures apart from me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that. And also, I don't know how common that surname, Praljak, is in the Croatian language, but definitely I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have put on the ELMO 3D 14-003. Could the usher please remove or -- 3D 14-003. Excuse me. 3D 00340. 3D 00340. Excuse me. Thank you. Witness, here we see a satellite photograph of an area of Mostar, Potoci is towards the north. We see the river here. And at the very top of the picture we see a small riverbed my question is can you recall there was a bridge called Bijela at the very top of this picture, near -- over the river Neretva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a Bijela bridge which was along the route that was taken by the humanitarian convoys taking humanitarian aid to the centre of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the engineers of your battalion repair the road around this river channel after the bridge was -- was damaged and make the road between Mostar and Jablanica passable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my tour of duty in Bosnia, no. But the next task force did in fact undertake repair work on the bridge in order to be able to use at that route. Not my task force, the one that came after us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was not about repairs to the bridge, but it was different. When the bridge was built there was a macadam road going around this arm of the river. Did you repair that road so that even without using the bridge the main road Mostar-Jablanica-Konjic would be passable and was that road always passable for UNHCR convoys going towards Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That route was no longer used when the Bijela bridge was blown up and when the Mostar situation did not allow us to use that route. So we used an alternative route and not that one. Hence I do not recall any, any sappers repairing that route. This is what I remember. However, I do also remember that later, the following task force or the task force that followed ours did some repair work, and I said this yesterday. Some Slovenian engineers tried to repair the bridge and were unable to do so because of the combat situations. They had no access. They could gain no access to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I regret I can't show you all the reports about travelling to Jablanica and Konjic and so on, although it says that 250 metres of macadam road were repaired by SpaBat engineers. But on this map, in relation to this area where Bijela was, where were the HVO positions on these green hills? Can you indicate that? The positions of the HVO in relation to the Bijela bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, thank you. My next question: A previous witness, and we do have the right to refer to previous witnesses, this was Christopher Beese, wrote several reports saying that there was marching in front of the barracks in Ljubuski. Was there any HVO barracks in Ljubuski, any kind of barracks belonging to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but memory tends to fail me. I don't know the area so well as you do, obviously. If I had reports in hand, the ones that I drafted, I could recall other things, but speaking like this, off-the-cuff, it's difficult whether in Ljubuski there were HVO barracks or not. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, sir. Electricity's frequently mentioned when problems in mutual relations are spoken of, so I'll ask you the following: Do you know where one of the largest transmitters was in a place called Cule on the road going to Mostar from your base a little before Hum hill? This was a transformer station and a representative of the European Community was killed there, after which they withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina, a large transformer station in Cule on the right-hand side. My question is: Do you know what the importance was for electricity supplies on an extended area of that transformer station? It had 220 kilowatts, 110 kilowatts, and 240 kilowatts, and a -- three huge transformers of 300 megawatts and one of 150 megawatts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about the problems with electricity supplies. I can say nothing about the data you're giving me about the megawatts of the Cule transformers or transformer. I know there was an important transformer there, but I have no more information than that. But it was a problem, electricity supply was a problem in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although this was one of the biggest centres for the 400 kilowatt network in the former Yugoslavia, and it was completely destroyed by the Serbs, you were not familiar with the problems in electricity supply that such a loss represents. It's worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole issue of infrastructure was the responsibility of an engineers officer who had come straight from the UNPROFOR headquarters. As it happened, he was a Spaniard. He travelled around the area, and he dealt with infrastructure, roads, electricity, and sometimes he did come around the Spanish area. But it was not part of our responsibility and therefore I can say very little about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that Their Honours will ask me for the basis. It was completely destroyed. Not only this plant but all long distance links between the large transformer stations and the power plants on the river Neretva were destroyed, and not a single organisation that was in the area took into account the incredible destruction of that network.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you are to ask questions. You are bombarding us with information our witness has stated he knows nothing about. It's not correct use of -- of -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Do you know that three hydroelectric power plants on the river of Neretva existed, Jablanica, Grabovica, and Salakovac, and that these were in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? They're all a little to the north of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did know that they had the -- that the Muslim army had the key to those installations you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How then -- thank you. How, then, with three electric power plants did it come about that eastern Mostar had no electricity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking technical questions that I cannot answer. I'm not an electrical engineer. I don't know how electricity supply was -- was organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't answer that question in technical terms, but when you were in Mostar, did you know that the electricity supply would be cut or that there was no electricity? Is this something that you experienced or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Electricity supply was a problem in Mostar -- problem, sorry, in Mostar. Generally the Muslims, being enemies of their enemies, did not cut off the electricity, but there were some blackouts. Generators were widely used for street lighting and lighting in houses because often there was no electricity supply. But it's not something that I poured into in-depth nor was I was in charge of that question, so I can say very little about it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in Medjugorje often have power cuts and shortages of electricity? You had your own aggregates, but did you receive electricity from the cables, and how often was there no electricity coming from electrical cables?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot with malfrequency [phoen], because we had our own electricity generator when necessary. When necessary we always had electricity supply. But I do not recall. It was not something that I was dealing with. Yes, there were electricity blackouts, but how often I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you visited there, were you familiar with the fact because of your general understanding of the situation that the total electric network of Bosnia-Herzegovina up to Zenica could not function without cooperation with Croatia for complicated technical reasons? Were you ever informed about that within the framework of this problem arising on the ground in order to avoid reaching the wrong conclusions? Did you hear that at any meeting or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate this is something that did not concern the Spanish Battalion. It was dealt with by the Sarajevo UNPROFOR headquarters. There were engineers who toured the area who came round and so on and so forth. We were given some information. I simply escorted those engineers, and that was the limit of my duties. So I cannot give you information. Anything I say is mere speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, it would perhaps be best to move on to another subject since on a number of occasions the witness has already told you that he wasn't the appropriate witness to answer such questions. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes. But to me it's important to hear that he knows nothing about it, Your Honours, because in the documents we have here, conclusions are made about electricity, and blame is laid for electricity shortages out of ignorance. So this answer is good enough for me. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you refer to the SpaBat document which concerns the subject of electricity. Perhaps that would refresh your memory. Perhaps it would see light.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, if I may assist, I think it's Prosecution document P 04423, where in paragraph 1.2, referring to the Mostar area, in the final part, and Mr. Praljak, please correct me if you think this is not the document you're referring to, it says, "We have to remember that the long-distance transmission lines are passing through Bijelo Polje and --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is reading too fast for the interpreter to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "-- Bijelo Polje and that a permanent cease-fire is a precondition for any repairs. At the same time, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have to ensure electric power supplies to the Croatian zone also because of the fact that they caused an interruption in electricity supplies." This is P 04423, and it's the comment -- one of the comments accompanying the passage concerning Mostar. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. As I have very little time left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a look at the document. If we do have the document, let's have a look at it very rapidly. I cannot see the reference to electricity. Ms. Alaburic, which item is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, the B/C/S and English versions of the document don't quite correspond to each other, so I can provide you with a reference that concerns the Croatian text. My colleague has just informed me that it's page 7 in the English version of the document. It's the third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's the first paragraph in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the fourth paragraph. It starts with the word "Comment." It's on page 7 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's page 5 in the Spanish version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you can see the paragraph in the Spanish text now. It starts with the words "recordemus" et cetera. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, no problem. I can see it perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, put your question to the witness so that he can answer it rapidly. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is do you know anything about this matter and can you testify that this is actually stated in the SpaBat report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This SpaBat report is a true document, a valid document. It's an intelligence report. It tells about the problems in the area, although it wasn't our problem. We simply reflected the comments and needs of the two parties. We were in touch with both parties, with both sides. The electricity supply problem was a perennial problem between the two sides, that's true, but I can add no more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I haven't got much time left, so I'll move on. When a mortar shell is fired, is it possible to see this from any point in Mostar, if the mortar is located behind Mount Hum, et cetera? Is it possible to see such a mortar shell being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you see at the moment when the mortar is shot with a radar, with modern means that armies have, yes, you can locate where it came from. If know where the mortar has impacted on the ground, as happened with Lieutenant Munoz, we could see the impact because they were clearly seen on the macadam road. You can then calculate from where the shot was fired and the distance, and a study was in fact undertaken on the basis of the impact prints on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I completely agree with you, sir. It's not possible to determine where the shell, the mortar shell, came from. It's not possible because the shell is not visible. You can't see it. And on the whole, it can't be heard. Only an analysis of the impact of the shell can help one determine the origin of the shell. Would you agree with my two previous conclusions? If you can't see the shell, and if there is noise you can't hear it either, you can't determine its origin on the basis of the sound, and therefore the only possibility of determining the origin of the shell is an analysis -- is to carry out an analysis of the impact of the shell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you are now acting as your own expert, it seems. It is not putting a question. You are giving expert testimony on ballistics and the like. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, this isn't a matter of complicated philosophy. The witness knows about such things. He can say, "You're not right," or "you are right, Mr. Praljak." I'm just asking him how it's possible to determine such a thing. There is, in my opinion, only one way of doing this and the witness can deny what I've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without being ballistics experts, you are nevertheless, both of you, high-ranking officers. According to what Mr. Praljak said when you examine the impact of a shell, when you examine the debris or the crater formed, it is then possible to determine where this shell was fired from. That is what Praljak seems to be saying. Do you agree with him as far as that point of view is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's exactly what I said before. If we know where the shell impacted, if it's on the field it would be more difficult. As it happened, this shot that we're talking about, in fact, landed on the road, and therefore we could perfectly see where it had fallen. It was fairly easy to determine where the shell had come from. It was fairly easy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what basis did you arrive at the conclusion that the shell had been fired from the Hum hill, rather, from behind the Hum hill. Mr. Praljak, do continue. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question, sir. We do remember the late Mr. Abasiar [phoen], but we don't know whether the bullet 7.62 calibre came from the left side, 50 metres -- from a distance of 50 metres away or from the other side, from the side of the building at a distance of 700 metres, as you said. Wouldn't it be possible to carry out an experiment at the site, to put a flak jacket on something that resembled a human body? I won't go into detailed descriptions of how this can be done. And then from a distance of 700 metres you could have tried to open fire to see whether a 7.62-calibre bullet had sufficient kinetic force to penetrate both the front and back part of the flak jacket which was a quality flak jacket which was 15 or 16 kilos in weight and could it -- that have resulted in the death of the officer. Was that not possible? My question is why didn't your battalion carry out such an experiment to determine who the military idiot was who killed your officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did investigate the death of the official, obviously, because it was quite a blow to us. The jacket wasn't bullet-proof but a fragment proof or flak-proof bullet vest. It's not as resistant as the bullet-proof one. Akarasi [phoen] used by the Spanish army, used also by snipers, strong enough, 600 metres away to actually get right -- get through a fragment proof vest on both sides. It's extremely strong, and it can pierce the vest. You don't actually have to carry out that experiment physically. You could have tried to test angles or trajectories, et cetera. Nonetheless, my colleague who went to the sniper site in order to get to that sniper site he actually laid his life on the line because he was under fire, and he had to be constantly protecting himself in order to get to the site from which the sniper shot. So it was extremely difficult to carry out any kind of test or experiment there. Constantly under fire, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just said something that adds more precise information. You will said that the lieutenant was wearing a jacket that was short of shrapnel proof rather than bullet-proof. How is that the case? You knew there were snipers. Why wasn't your colleague -- why hadn't your colleague been provided with a bullet-proof vest. But whether he had a bullet-proof vest or not, given the calibre used by the sniper, the result would have been the same. Is that how I'm to understand the answer you have given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not really. Had he been wearing a bullet-proof vest he would not have died. But it's -- it's the same old thing over and over again, you see. It's eternal story. You cannot issue a bullet-proof vest to every single member on the battalion. They're hard to come by. They're not really totally sophisticated yet. They're not completely bullet-proof even though they're supposed to be. And it's cumbersome for soldiers. Most armies still use the anti-flak or anti-fragment vest which is -- which is normal issue to a soldier rather than an anti -- or the bullet-proof vest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have -- Mr. Praljak, have you now concluded or do you have other questions you'd like to put to the witness? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm just sorry that I didn't know that the investigation the soldier was wearing was the one usually worn -- was not the one that's usually worn. So anyway. I'm sorry about that. And thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now 10.35. We'll have our 20-minute break now and we'll resume after 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. It seems that I made a slight mistake as far as time is concerned. Petkovic's Defence will have 90 minutes and Coric's Defence 45 minutes, which means that Mr. Petkovic's Defence team has until the next break, and then Coric's -- Mr. Coric's Defence team will have 45 minutes after the break. Please go ahead. It's now 11.00, and you have until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good day to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. My name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and I represent General Milivoj Petkovic. Witness, first of all I would like to put several questions to you that directly relate to parts of the indictment that the Prosecution believes you might be able to help us with. Do you remember that in December, 1997, you spoke to -- in January, correction, you spoke to investigators from the trial about certain subjects that have been addressed here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The month concerned was November.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to correct something. I said November, whereas that is not what is stated in the transcript. I mentioned November.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made a statement before this Chamber. I do not recall the date. It could have been November, during which I stated as to the knowledge that I had or I did not have during my time there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to refresh your memory, remind you of what you said with regard to my client. On that occasion, you said the following, and I quote: "I escorted Mr. Petkovic or I accompanied him when he went to missions in Jablanica. My impression was that he did not wield much power. I can provide you with an example. We were stopped at an HVO checkpoint, and Colonel Morales asked Petkovic to tell his soldiers to let us pass through. The HVO soldier refused to do so until he had received an order from his immediate superior." I'll now skip two sentences, and then the following two sentences are as follows, and I quote: "Petkovic was on good terms with Halilovic, too, and it was my impression that Petkovic didn't take any decisions." And in relation to this, my question is as follows: Can you now confirm before this Trial Chamber the impression that you had with regard to my client?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you have to distinguish between the decision-making capacity at general headquarters level within the structures of the HVO, whether it is the Ministry of Defence or its headquarters, and also the command power in terms of isolated troops or isolated units placed in the field. But of course in terms of the field, the discipline was also not terribly good within the Croat army during that time in November and the soldiers on leave would obey direct orders from their immediate superiors. And General Petkovic was not often listened to or paid attention to. But in terms of saying that he did not have the power, well, he did not have much decision-making capacity, and that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as the second part or the other part of the indictment is concerned, I have two previous questions I'd like to put to you. Did you ever attend a meeting of the Croatian leadership of Herceg-Bosnia of the HVO armed forces and of political leaders from the republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether I attended one of their meetings, meetings of the leadership? If I attended one of their meetings, the answer is no. It was a meeting with them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The question concerns their meetings. My conclusion is that your answer to my question is negative. And the only conclusion I can draw is that if you did not attend such meetings, you cannot testify about whether my client attended such meetings, and that is the purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. I don't know what meetings General Petkovic attended within his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now, Witness, I would like us to clarify some of your statements that concerned the HVO Main Staff in various contexts, although you also discussed people and duties that really weren't performed, and all of this took place within a body called the HVO Main Staff. And as a result, I believe we should clarify who you have in mind when you say the command or the HVO headquarters. Tell us, do you know who the Supreme Commander of the HVO armed forces was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first times, I think it was generally General Petkovic, and many negotiations, many decisions were organised or done with him. He was the organiser as the commander of the HVO forces. After that, it was General Praljak who took over from him and who took over the command of those forces. But during many occasions decisions were not on in terms of military issues, and often the negotiations, the most important negotiations during which we managed to achieve more things or more results was directly with the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The deputy minister of defence, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, the Supreme Command of the HVO armed forces was Mr. Mate Boban. Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Praljak were the chiefs of the Main Staff, or they were the first men in the HVO Main Staff. When you mentioned Mr. Bozic, and you say that you met him in the HVO Main Staff, when you refer to the command of the Main Staff do you actually have the Ministry of Defence in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters and the Main Staff or the headquarters of the unit -- I'm referring to military people, not civilians, so the Supreme Commander was General Petkovic, and his superior would have been some civilian, perhaps in this case the minister or deputy minister of defence and, naturally, the president of that republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your answer, I can draw the conclusion that you in fact did not have detailed knowledge of the relationship between three bodies, the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, the Main Staff of the HVO, and the Ministry of Defence or, rather, the government of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, normally we tend to simplify matters and we deduct from what is there, and we apply our knowledge in relation to what we know from our own government or our own flow charts, and we take that to the country we are assigned to and it happens to work along that basis. It was a Western country, it was an army, a Yugoslav army that followed those characteristics. I don't know whether that was the relationship but I thought it was very similar to the relationship that takes place in other countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Witness, whether the army in your country, for instance, functions in such a way that the state bodies or, rather, the civilian authorities decide on matters within their jurisdiction, whereas your army does not take part in making such decisions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally in my country indeed the decisions are taken by the government of the nation, and they're civilians, and they're advised by the military command in terms of military issues, in terms of the decisions, operational decisions that are to be carried out by the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you say that the civilian authorities is the body that brings in decisions, that is to say that they decide whether agreements on cease-fires will be concluded or not, and whether hostilities will cease or not, or whether the strategic and tactical interests of the country are different and don't warrant that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally I understand that it has to be the civilian authorities that have to take those decisions. Decisions are taken at all levels, and one is responsible for the decisions ascribed to us, but obviously decisions are taken by the civilians in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that on the territory of Herceg-Bosna as well, what happened was that the civilian authorities would make the corresponding decisions and that after then the military commanders would conclude agreements and issue the corresponding orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'm going to object. I think -- I haven't objected up till now. I think the witness, given his background and experience is able to make some broad statements, but now I think this question says, Can you confirm that on the territory of Herceg-Bosna as well what happened. I think now we're getting into whether this witness is an expert to talk about how this actually functioned in Herceg-Bosna. Unless additional foundation is laid, I don't think it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was listening carefully to your questions and to the answers as well, and you are getting to a crucial problem, and you say that -- which is about the control the civilian authorities had over the military. Now, the problem here is that this witness -- is this witness the right person to answer questions like that? You asked him what the case was in Spain, and he said that the military authorities depend the on the civilian authorities. He answered that one. Now you want to ask the same question and apply it to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, there we risk -- run the risk of wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I, of course, agree with your observation, and I do not consider that we will be wasting time, because this witness and the units to which he belonged, and the documents of those units, can provide us with the relevant answers to the questions. And the comment made by my learned friend of the Prosecution I consider to be completely unfounded because the documents that he provided to us also represent military commanders and civilian authorities. And I'd just like to refer to Prosecution Exhibit P 01717, and that is an operations diary for the 19th of April when, in Medjugorje, a meeting was held among others with General Morillon and Thelman [phoen], with Petkovic and Halilovic, and the representatives of two armies were represented as representatives of Mr. Ganic and Mr. Boban. So that means the representatives of the power and authorities in Sarajevo and the authorities in Mostar. And from that it would emerge that the meeting in Medjugorje came after a political agreement had been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, to clarify my -- if -- then I suggest that counsel puts the specific document to the witness then instead of talking about broad conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Put the documents to the witness so he can see them, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document and what I quoted just now was just a pretext for me to show my own documents to the witness. And I'd like on e-court to show the following document: 4D 00302. It is a document which unfortunately we do not have in Spanish. We have the B/C/S -- or, rather the Croatian and English version. So the document number is 4D 00302.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your -- or, rather, witness this is an order by my client which was sent out to the UN headquarters in Kiseljak among others. The date of the decision is the 17th of August, 1993, and at this point in time I'm just interested in the introduction in which my client refers to the Supreme Commander of the armed forces and also the president of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban. And the introductory portion of this order reads as follows, and I quote: "Mr. Mate Boban at a -- at the meeting in Geneva once again reiterated his and our approval on the unhindered movement of the United Nations forces in the territory of BiH." I'd now like to ask that the witness be shown another document about this same topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise for -- excuse me. I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can see the document, but what's the -- what's your question on this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please be allowed to show the witness the second document first and then put my question? My question is how the political decisions came before the activities of the commanders of the army, and that was my introductory question, in fact. So may we have the next document put to the witness. I'd just like to draw your attention to the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- we continue to have our objection. I fully agree that counsel has read the document accurately. I fully agree that this document is also a Prosecution exhibit. We don't doubt its authenticity, it comes from the HVO archive, it bears the stamp on the B/C/S original in the upper right corner. I do not dispute either the authenticity of the document or the counsel has read it correctly but it appears what counsel is going to do is simply put certain documents before the witness that the witness has no personal knowledge of and then try to argue him into making some conclusions based on the documents that she has shown him, and I don't think that's proper examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me make the following observation first. I see that the addressees, that is to say where the document was delivered to, says "United Nations, Kiseljak." So it is quite possible that at the level of the UN system in Kiseljak this was transmitted to the different areas where UNPROFOR was located. So he might have known about this. So perhaps it would be better to let the Defence ask the question first and then we can see. And, Defence counsel, you can ask the witness whether he's seen this or not and that would avoid objections from the Prosecution which wastes a lot of our time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to ask that the time used by Mr. Scott for his interventions should not be deducted from my own time allotted for cross-examination and that during objections from the Prosecution my time is not deducted but that time made up for. I'd like us to show the witness one nor document and I'll be asking questions with related to both documents because, Your Honour, at this point in time with respect to these two documents it is not essential that he -- I don't want to introduce them into evidence, it's just a basis for my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead but quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is 4D 00303. It is an order, again. The number is 4D 00303. As I was saying, it is an order from my client or by my client, General Petkovic, sent to SpaBat in Medjugorje. It is dated the 17th of August, 1993. And I'm just interested in the introduction, and it says: "On the basis of agreement between Mr. Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic on the evacuation of wounded and injured from Nova Bila and Mostar," my client issues the following order ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is as follows -- from these documents, in view of the fact that my learned friend Mr. Scott told me to ask questions on the basis of my own documents and not his documents, my question is as follows: In your understanding of the relationship between civilian and military authorities, do these documents show that in Herceg-Bosna as well as in your own country, for example, the civilian authorities were those who made the relevant decisions after which the military commanders issued their own relevant orders following on from that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that that ought to be the case but I do not have any confirmation that that is the case. I understand the decisions ought to have come from Mate Boban. From what it says it seems to be able to wish him to maintain this structure of the decision-making -- the political decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd now like to move on to another area relating to the control of passage and movement. Witness, I'm sure you have a great deal of experience about the events that take -- took place in other areas of war, in other theatres of operation. So I'd like to ask you the following: To the best of your knowledge, the control of roads, is that something that is usual and compulsory everywhere where there's a war conflict going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- not obligatory. It's convenient or advisable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain why you think it's a good idea to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is necessary to check the -- the national territory. It is possible to follow up movements of goods, and you need to know what is taking place in the area. We're talking about areas of conflict, areas of war. This is elementary information. It is elementary or basic to undertake certain checkpoints of -- over the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, is it precisely for that reason that along with the presence of your own battalion or, rather, the United Nations, between the warring parties, that is to say the Croats and the Muslims, an agreement was signed relating to the control of roads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to highlight that the Spanish Battalion never came in between the two parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the translation on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Quite obviously you didn't understand me. I was referring to an agreement between Commanders Halilovic and Petkovic dated the 12th of May, 1993. And I'd like us to show the witness this document. It is document 4D 00070, and it is an agreement between General Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic signed on the 12th of May, 1993, in the presence of General Morillon and Ambassador Thebault. And in point 1 of that agreement, third section, it refers to the control of roads, supervision of roads and checkpoints. Control of routes. Now, in view of the fact, Witness, that you have already explained to us the reasons for controlling routes and the justification for the existence of checkpoints, there's no need to waste time discussing this agreement in detail, but what I will do is to observe that checkpoints are something that existed legally and legitimately, and they do in war zones. Now I come to my question. Witness, to the best of your knowledge did the BH army control the routes on territory under its control, and did it also have checkpoints along the way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, along the route going up to Jablanica area when the Spanish Battalion arrived there the checkpoints of the armija and of the HVO would alternate because there would be areas fighting the -- the other parties either by the armija or the HVO, and there were checkpoints from one of those two armies. Then they disappeared. When the Muslim army took over in the Croat area, then the Croats remained, and then there were checkpoints to control and obviously if you want the movement on the other party as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question. I don't want to take up time, but I would like you to specify. Article 1 of that agreement for the cease-fire, it states that control of routes will be maintained by civilian police only. And at the end of that paragraph it says that military units will not exercise control. So that mean that when there is a cease-fire agreed upon by two belligerent sides, do the military units give up control of the routes? That's what this agreement means. If an agreement is reached, then the military units do not exercise control. Would that be right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many other agreements that were signed up until 1995. There were just, they were just worth the weight of the paper. They didn't really mean anything. And in terms of what General Morillon or the willingness that we had for a cease-fire to actually take place between the two warring parties, well, this meant that practically every fortnight we would end up signing cease-fire agreements that really didn't have any power because they were not respected by any of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, may I then conclude that the BH army also had checkpoints? In your reports you refer to checkpoints of the BH army, which due to -- you were not able to pass through because you were not allowed to and, therefore, you couldn't go to the area under your responsibility. I would just like to clarify one point. The area of Dreznica, if you remember, was the area of Dreznica under the control of -- well, this is a question which relates to the Prosecution document P 01717 for the 10th of May and the 26th of May. And my question -- I'm asking the question for the following reasons because I'm trying to anticipate the objection Mr. Scott is going to make. Because the possibility of passing through Dreznica does not state it was a checkpoint under the responsibility and the control of the BH army as opposed to the checkpoints of the HVO, for example, in the report that relates to the 8th of July where it says that there was an HVO checkpoint. So that is the justification for my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not my objection. But again, our continuing objection is to counsel giving evidence or making assertions that are not in fact put to the witness. On page 49, line 1, Ms. Alaburic says, "Witness, may I then conclude that the BH army also had checkpoints." Probably not very controversial, I suspect. "You refer to checkpoints the BH army which due to -- you were not able to pass through because you were not allowed to and therefore you couldn't go to the area under your responsibility." And then she goes on to a question. The witness is never given a chance to respond. It's not a question. It's simply an assertion by counsel, which is not evidence, and which the witness has had no opportunity to react to. So it's that kind of a thing that we continue to object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before we arrive at a conclusion, ask your preliminary questions, and then looking at the document you can say, "Do you answer in the affirmative or negative, based on the document?" But otherwise, we might not have the witness here at all. We'd just let you go on talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not able to control the interpretation, but perhaps there's been a misunderstanding. I deduced my observation from documents which were introduced by the Prosecutor and on the basis of documents that the Prosecution -- examination -- used in the examination-in-chief. So I think the contents of those documents is something that we have already been through. So I didn't feel that I had to present them to the witness for him to be able to confirm their authenticity or anything with else with respect to these documents. So I think that those documents are a premise for my own questions, the groundwork for my question, and that is why I went on to observe the problems that existed in passing checkpoints in the Dreznica area because this is something that was contained in a SpaBat report, and after that my direct question was as follows: Were those checkpoints held and controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time we went from one zone to another one there were controls. An HVO where the HVO zone ended and the appropriate one where the other zone started. Problems could be presented by both parties, one side or whoever was interested in creating problems, but there were always controls when one was travelling from one zone to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I completely understand, but I'd just like to know who held the checkpoints in Dreznica. If you don't remember, Witness, we can move on. We don't need to spend too much time on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably both sides. When the HVO zone came to an end there would be HVO forces, and when the Muslim zone -- where the Muslim zone started there would be Muslims in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we show the witness Prosecution Exhibit P 01717 now, please, for the 10th of May. In the Croatian text it is on page 9, and in the English version it is on page 59. There's a portion which states as follows: "During the night, the BH army took control of the checkpoint at the bridge in Dreznica. This checkpoint has been established and makes it difficult for our vehicles to pass through." This same document, for the 26th of May, and in Croatian it is on page 19 and in English it is on page -- just one moment. Let me check. In English it will be on page 72, seventh line where it speaks about the BH army checkpoint at Dreznica. And throughout the document it mentions Dreznica as a BH army checkpoint. Now, sometimes when a document refreshes your memory you can answer the question, so I'd like to repeat my question. The 10th of May, was Dreznica in the hands of the BH army, under BH army control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, the Dreznica area was under Muslim control, but there was an HVO pocket which had an entrance on the Dreznica area, and hence on the 26th of May entry it is said that the BH army allowed -- allowed people to go through if the HVO did likewise. But the checkpoint was a BH checkpoint, no doubt, in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In P 01717, the operative diary, Prosecution Exhibit, if I read the diary carefully there was a ban on movement in the direction of Mostar which is mentioned for the first time in the report for the 11th of July, 1993. That's the first time that was ever mentioned. Could you confirm that up until that date there was no ban on movement in the direction of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Movement was -- Mostar -- as from when hostilities broke out in May it was very difficult. Some days we could go through, some days we could not. It depended on operations or on God knows what. We don't know. And the operations were what the HVO decided, and total prohibition, direct prohibition from the HVO came. Amongst other things, they were infringing, of course, the agreement with the United Nations, but we were told that all movement was prohibited as from that date. Hence the entry in the logbook. It does not mean that before freedom of movement was easy, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you cannot hear me speaking in my own language. In my own language I stressed the word "ban" or "prohibition" precisely because I anticipated the difficulties of entering Mostar in the period following the 9th of May. I am fully aware of the difficulties and the temporary inability to enter Mostar in the preceding period, so my question referred to a prohibition on movement in the direction of Mostar with the date of the 11th of July. So was there a prohibition in place as of mid-July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date. If the logbook which we have could show the actual 11th of July date, well, if the logbook says that the prohibition dates as from that day, then I confirm what is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On that day -- in the report for that day the prohibition is mentioned for the first time. I would need a lot of time to prove that there was no such prohibition in place on the previous days. Therefore, I will accept your response. And in order to make the best possible use of my time, I will move on to another topic relating to humanitarian aid convoys. Witness, to the best of your knowledge, in principle did a convoy have to receive approval for travel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, that is so. UNHCR, in order to allow travel or to have their convoys travel, some did get in touch with whoever needed to be got in touch in order to have travel permit, and I believe travel permits were requested. The Spanish escorts, once they knew about the itinerary of the convoy, joined the convoy in order to escort it throughout its journey.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this travel permit had to include information about the vehicles in the convoy, the persons who would be in the convoy, the type and amount of goods to be transported, the time of departure of the convoy and its route?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I do not know what relations UNHCR had with the two sides, but I do know what contacts and what relations we had in order to provide security. We had a control officer in Metkovic where the UNHCR warehouses were situated, and we were told about the day, time, number of lorries, and the journey itinerary, and we escorted those lorries or UNHCR vehicles. The relation of UNHCR with the two sides I know nothing about, but I suppose they would provide information too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I wish to show you P 01717. It's an operations log for the 25th of May. In Croatian it's on page 18. I do apologise. The 26th of May. It's the first passage referring to the 26th of May. Here it is on the screen. This first passage, yes, we have it in Spanish also, reads as follows: "Isolated rifle shots could be heard in Mostar during the day. Another attempt has been made today to get a humanitarian aid convoy into the Muslim quarter in the city. The passage through a checkpoint was banned [as interpreted] by the HVO. They insisted on checking the cargo first, and then, once they had done that, to discuss who would receive the cargo. Finally the UNHCR representative agreed that the convoy could pass the next day, but that 60 per cent of the cargo would go to Croats and 40 per cent to the Muslims." I will show you two reports of yours from this document and then I will put my question. So for the month of June, the 10th of June, the 11th, 12th, and 13th of June, the same statement is made in all four reports. If we can take a look at the 10th of June. It's line 4. In the 11th of June also. And you say that all UNHCR convoys have been -- are not coming because the routes to Central Bosnia have been closed off. For June in your reports there is not a single note about the humanitarian convoy for Mostar. And just another part of this document. With reference to the 17th of July, the last paragraph, which reads: "The UNHCR has stopped all convoys because the HVO demanded that a certain percentage of the aid be distributed to both communities before they issued the permit for passage through their territory." In connection with these statements in your reports, my question is as follows: If in May, 1993, an UNHCR humanitarian convoy was able to enter east Mostar, provided they left 60 per cent of the cargo to the Croats, what happened in July which meant that UNHCR would not go to Eastern Mostar? They refused to do so at any cost.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whilst I've been here, we said that there were some 40 days, two months, I'm not sure exactly about the time, there were then days from beginning of July till August when the passage through -- to Mostar was in fact barred and, therefore, no convoys reached Mostar. But I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll clarify. Witness, in the SpaBat reports for the 17th of July, 1993, it says that the UNHCR cancelled all convoys or suspended all the convoys because the HVO demanded that a certain percentage of aid be distributed to both communities. Two months previously, however, the same organisation brought aid to Mostar, and according to your reports also gave aid to the Croatian side. So logically the question follows, what happened to make the UNHCR change its policy? According to your reports, the situation in Eastern Mostar was not -- well it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, "was such."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that the UN should have delivered some aid and what you report for the 17th of July has a direct bearing on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, counsel expresses her view that UNHCR should have. It's her view that they should have delivered some aid. I'm not sure that is particularly relevant to the courtroom. Thirdly, it is perhaps not this witness that should explain the policy or decisions made by UNHCR. It's a completely separate organisation, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In response to the question, I would notice that there was a convoy that entered, the Muslims and Croats shared the load, and Defence is asking you, and this is something that the Judges are interested in too, the Defence is asking you whether there were no other convoys over a period of several weeks after that. Did you have an answer or not? This is what interests us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In May there was relative freedom of movement to the Mostar area, and we did get convoys in, in May. In June, eastern Mostar was closed for almost two months. Now, this does not mean that no convoys got through to Central Bosnia. To Central Bosnia there were convoys. Not to eastern Mostar, but yes, to Central Bosnia.
