And it was later on, the 17th of July, when my memory's refreshed, that from the moment when the HVO demanded a certain percentage of the cargo UNHCR decided to cancel the rest of the convoys to Central Bosnia. The UNHCR warehouses were in Metkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to be more precise, once more you said it was a ban, that someone had banned the convoys. Who banned them? At least the French translation said banned. Were they suspended or were they banned? What do you say in Spanish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Suspended. UNHCR decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's the UNHCR that suspended the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely my question. I think we have now clarified this part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will now put a few questions to you in connection with Sovici and Doljani. I assume that these two place names mean something to you. Perhaps to start when we could look at P 02192. That is a report for the 3rd of May, 1993, and on page 1, in the section entitled "Jablanica," which is on page 3 in Croatian and page 4 in English, the first sentence of the paragraph reads: "The town of Doljani, completely destroyed and burnt down, was the first to be visited." Do you see that sentence, Witness? The town of Doljani is completely destroyed and burnt, and you visited it first with Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not visit that village. I was not at that visit at that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any other information about the source or who it was that wrote this sentence in the report? I'll tell you why I'm asking this. Because from the census of 1991, I have information here according to which the village of Doljani is predominantly Croatian. About two-thirds of the population were Croats. So I wanted to put some detailed questions about this part of the report which says that Doljani is completely destroyed and burnt down. However, if you have no further information about this, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the situation is clear. I have not travelled to all the places the Spanish Battalion travelled to. I can be responsible of the documents because I know they have been drafted by colleagues of mine, and, given the reliability of these documents, I can confirm that what is contained therein is the truth, but it does not mean that I drafted the document or that I was present at all events. In some cases I was present, in some I was not. In this particular case, I was not present. I did travel to Jablanica to the meeting that was taking place, but I did not join the meeting -- sorry, I did not join the visit to the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I wanted to ask you a few questions about what it was that Generals Petkovic and Halilovic agreed on in connection to the populations and Sovici and Doljani. So I will put a few documents to you very quickly, and I will try to put the most relevant questions. Could we show 4D 00321 to the witness. It's very short. And we also have it in English. We have it in English and Croatian but not in Spanish. So I will read it out. This is a short letter from General Petkovic to the commander of the HVO in Doljani, whose name is Stipe Polo, where it says, I quote: "In Doljani and Sovici, release all the civilians found there. Keep the able-bodied men." The next document is 4D 00308. This is a document of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It comes from the Croatian state archives. Unfortunately, we still do not have a translation into English. The document is in Croatian. I see it on the screen. And around the middle of that document it says -- and this is a document issued by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I quote: "Tomorrow, an unconditional evacuation of the civilian population from Doljani and Sovici has been agreed upon." I'll put one more document. 4D 00312. We also have the text in English. It is a document disclosed to us by the Prosecution, where my client puts a question to the HVO in Doljani, asking whether "five buses have arrived in Sovici and Doljani to evacuate the population (the greens)" I'll explain that later, "in the direction of Jablanica," and if they have, where have they come from? My question is as follows: Did you learn from your colleagues or in any other way what Generals Halilovic and Petkovic agreed on with respect to the civilian populations in Sovici and Doljani? It follows from these documents that they would be transported to the territory they wished to go to, but do you yourself have any knowledge of this? Is there anything you can tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have vague memories because I was not directly involved in that operation. If I were to read the logbook and the entries for those dates, I'd probably remember more. But basically an agreement was reached whereby the civilian personnel from the Croat villages was going to be allowed to leave by bus to be transported to a Croat zone where they would be safe. Basically that's what was agreed. I can say no more. It was an agreement between the two generals, Halilovic and Petkovic, reached at Jablanica, hence the tour around the villages to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the translation was correct, or the interpretation, you mentioned Croatian villages. At that bev -- Sovici and Doljani were Croatian villages. Could you clarify whether you were referring to the two villages of Sovici and Doljani regardless of whose they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was referring to those villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I have a few questions about Muslims in the ranks of the HVO. To the best of your knowledge, in the ranks of the HVO were there any Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Bosnia and we took charge of the mission, the HVO army was a Bosnian Croat army. They were mixed, or mingled, although the headquarters were separate. But, yes, we did learn that some Muslims did continue belonging to the HVO army. We have no names nor when this happened, but we knew of Muslims in the HVO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about whether the Muslims in the HVO were really loyal soldiers of the army they belonged to, or did any problems arise in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a personal opinion. I have no information. I could give an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I think your opinion would be valuable to us, so please tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if he is going to give an opinion and I haven't objected to that yet, but can we have the foundation, lay the foundation before we get the opinion so we know whether there is, in fact, any basis for expressing such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What is the purpose of your question? You have a document that would allow one to establish that there were Muslims in the HVO, to establish whether these Muslims were loyal or not. We have such a document. So then why don't you show the witness the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do have a document. It's a SpaBat document referring to this topic. I felt it would be more useful for all of us to hear this witness's observations and opinions. I believe we have a right to hear his opinion because every SpaBat report ends with a comment which is, in fact, an opinion. If you think we could go in the other order, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. Ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I have understood correctly, the public Prosecutor wanted to know on what the opinion was based. That was actually your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So could you first say on what basis did you form the opinion and then what the opinion is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you my opinion on the basis of the information I had at the time. My duties did not include intelligence duties. These reports, which the Defence counsel is talking about, are, from the comments she's made, reports from the Intelligence Unit, not from my unit. But I knew of what was said at the meetings and the general opinion that existed in the Spanish Battalion at the time, and on this I can base my personal opinion, which may not actual coincide to the letter with the SpaBat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion is that there may have been loyal Muslims, but as war developed amongst them, they probably stayed in HVO area because they were there, out of fear, because of family ties, or for a thousand different reasons. But as for loyalty, I think I would put that in the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now show P 04698. It's page 7 in the Croatian version, page 9 in the English version. And, Witness, it's page 37 to page 38 in the Spanish text. Page 9 in the English version, and 37 to 38 in the Spanish version. Fortunately, I don't know Spanish, and I can't check to see whether the page I referred to in the Spanish version is the right one, but the passage I want to show to the witness is as follows. Perhaps the interpreters could help us determine whether this is the relevant part. I quote, "What was expected happened at dawn on the 30th of June, at 3.45 to be precise. The BH army carried out an attack in the direction of the north and thus took the Tihomir Misic barracks in the area of Bijelo Polje north-east of the town. It seems that this action was carried out in the night between the 29th and the 30th of June when the Muslims within the lines of the HVO 3 brigade took over the Tihomir Misic and, rather, deserted the Tihomir Misic barracks together with their weapons in order to join the army of BH. The Muslims took this opportunity to move on to the north, and they reached Bijelo Polje." My question is as follows, and it directly relates to the indictment and to what my client is being charged with: Apart from this situation with the Muslims, do you have any knowledge according to by in certain other areas Muslims also fled or deserted? They fled from the HVO with or without their weapons, and the HVO would lose certain positions or certain locations because of betrayal among its own ranks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this -- yes. Well, my memory is being refreshed as I read this, but I don't remember this happening elsewhere. It may have happened. I know not. With this document in hand, and if I do read everything, obviously my memory would be better refreshed. This I remember, but I cannot actually answer your questions saying that there were other cases. I know not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could I be informed of the amount of time I still have since I'll have to skip certain areas. I'd like to know how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have 15 minutes, because then we will have the 20-minute break, and then Mr. Coric's Defence will have 45 minutes. Try to complete your cross-examination within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think I'll manage to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, at the beginning of the discussion, although we didn't follow this up because there were a number of interesting things mentioned, but at the beginning you also mentioned the existence of certain groups and individuals who acted in the field listening to their own lower command. There were certain actions that were carried out during which the Main Staff was bypassed. I think you also mentioned the problem of soldiers who held onto their weapons but were on leave in fact. They didn't have any tasks to carry out. So could you tell us anything more about such manifestations of wilful behaviour on the part of individuals or groups of individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the main problem or is the main problem with all armies, that is to say, how to control its personnel, its units, particularly when the command staff are not around or they're not under their control. And undoubtedly there was indiscipline, and there were individuals who I believe did take inappropriate action. I can share with you personal anecdotes. It's not important, but I could show you personal anecdotes which shows the lack of discipline with very many of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would be interested in hearing one or two personal anecdotes, as you labelled them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on my way back from Split, around the border area between Bosnia and Croatia there was a car accident. A Spanish accident, crashed against a Croat vehicle. We were surrounded by crowds, very many of them soldiers in battle fatigues. I don't know whether they were soldiers or not. In a threatening fashion. I in fact had got off the vehicle and talked to them. I was surrounded all the time. They tried to take my weapons from me. They tried to attack me, and they were for ever trying to get money out of us, Deutschmark. We were there for about one to two hours discussing with them. The Croat police was present at that incident. There were Croat officers present, too, who did not take part whatsoever in the incident, did not intervene, and gradually I managed to persuade them that the problem could be solved by having them come to the SpaBat barracks and read our insurance policies that would deal with the problem. But there were many, very many soldiers on leave. At -- the village was in fact celebrating its celebrations and I can tell you that I had a pretty rough time, pretty rough time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, at the beginning of your answer you said that all armies have such problems, all armies throughout the world. On the basis of your experience in other countries than includes the territory of the former Yugoslavia, could you tell us whether you noticed a difference of any kind between such problems in armies that have existed for decades, the armies that are well structured and have educated soldiers and armies where the army is in fact still being formed and structured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer would take a very long time. It's not a very concrete question, but it's a fundamental problem of armies, how to control the personnel when the chiefs, when the command staff are not around. This is what we tried to instil in them, that they have to obey discipline even if the staff, the chiefs of staff or the command staff are not around. This is achieved in some armies. In some armies it is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if an army is still being formed and ordinary citizens who have no education or in fact the soldiers, could we take it for granted that there would be such problems to a far greater extent than in a well-established army in which the rules are quite clear and well established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt. No doubt. A rapid mobilisation army made up of citizens, of course, would find it far more difficult to maintain discipline than other armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned soldiers on leave and pointed out that this was a particular problem. Did you know that the organisation of the HVO army was based on so-called shift work or, rather, soldiers, citizens, were soldiers for two weeks and then they were free citizens for the next two weeks? They would take their weapons home with them. I can see that you are nodding, so you are familiar with such a situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Ten days, not half a month but 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. They would have shiftwork. They would be on shift for 10 days. They didn't have a barracks. They wouldn't leave their weapons at certain location as is usually done in well-established armies, well established military structures. What they would do is they would take their weapons home with them. According to your own information, would this make it more likely that certain incidents might occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more difficult. What doubt can there be? It is more difficult to control personnel that go back to their villages with their weapons. If there's no well-organised military police in the rear lines in the rest areas. Of course it is more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only have one more question for you, Witness. Could you tell us when you arrived in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the area that your battalion is responsible for, and when you left that area, was the territory under the control of the ABiH a large or small one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the SpaBat area of responsibility, theoretically there was one single army. They were together. The armija and the HVO. They fought together against the Serbs. As time went on, those two armies split up and hostilities broke out. Two armies came into being, but the area in which we moved was basically controlled in the Croat areas by the HVO and in the Muslim areas the armija. I don't know whether this was your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. My question concerned the territory under the control of the Croatian army or, rather, of the Muslims. If I can extend my question to the area that was under the 2nd Battalion UNPROFOR. I assume you're also familiar with the reports at the level of UNPROFOR. In the area under the ABiH and the HVO, my question is in that entire area which was later to become the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from April 1993 up until September 1993, was the territory under the control of the ABiH increased or did that territory diminish? If you can't answer with certainty, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can talk about the SpaBat area. The rest of the areas were -- UNPROFOR was present and where there were variations I cannot talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I find this question very difficult. What is small? In relation to what? I would not know the criteria, but perhaps, Witness, you could compare. You say -- was the larger part of the territory to which you were assigned under the control of the Croatians or under the control of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no information on square metres or hectares, but the area around which we moved about, well, more area was controlled by the Croats than by the Muslims. Now, if we take a measuring tape, maybe I will be proved wrong, but this is my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify something. It's obvious that the interpretation into French was incorrect. My question didn't concern a large area or a small area. I wanted to know whether the territory under the control of the ABiH had been increased, whether it had been increased. I just wanted to know whether the ABiH carried out attacks to enlarge the amount of territory under its control. That was the purpose of my question, but the witness can't answer it. He can only talk about the area under his responsibility. Given that's the situation I won't continue with this subject, but I have one final question, Witness. You told us that you quite frequently saw representatives of Croatian civilian and military authorities. You quite frequently worked with them. You said that you'd been in the office in the Main Staff. Can you tell us at any point in time, regardless of whether it was Petkovic or Praljak who was the Supreme Commander, can you tell us whether you ever saw a photograph of Ante Pavelic in the office of the Supreme Command, and do you know who Ante Pavelic was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of Ante Pavelic, but I'm very much afraid that if I saw a photograph of him I couldn't recognise him. When I got there on a courtesy visit to Petkovic that's really all I did because normally speaking I would not visit the HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you see the photograph of anyone in that office hang on the wall? Did you see a photograph of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, I don't remember having seen any photographs at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you why I'm asking you this. The witness who was here before you said that in all -- almost all official premises of the HVO he saw the photograph of Ante Pavelic who was the top man in the Independent State of Croatia, which was state that existed at the time of the second world war and was close to Germany. I think you know something about that, and that's why I put this question to you. I wanted to know whether when you had contact with Croats in the territory of Herceg-Bosna you ever gained the impression that these people were in some way associated with Nazi or fascist ideologies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never discussed the matter of ideology with them, in any of my contacts with them. We never talked about ideology. We only talked about day-to-day problems. That was more than enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think my time is up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll now have our break, and we will resume at 10 to 1.00. The next Defence team will have 45 minutes at its disposal, and we must conclude by 1.45 because there is another hearing in the afternoon, and if we are late in adjourning, the Chamber that will be having a hearing in the afternoon will be angry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without wasting any more time, I'll give the floor to the next and last Defence counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The time we have been allotted for our team we shall divide up between myself and my client, Mr. Valentin Coric. Cross-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Dijana Tomasegovic Tomic, I am an attorney from Zagreb, and in this case I represent Mr. Valentin Coric. utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm all set.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine now. I'll introduce myself. My name is Dijana Tomasegovic Tomic. I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and in this case I'm counsel for Valentin Coric. To start before any cross-examination, I'd like to go back to the first part of the examination-in-chief and what you said there. I think it was on the 22nd of June when you appeared before this Tribunal for the first time, and I'd just like to remind you, I don't want to repeat what was already said, but at the time you talked about the reliability of SpaBat reports. Do you remember that? Do you remember addressing that matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whether I was asked about what was in the documents and I was asked what the meaning of that was, yes, I was asked about it. What the letters and numbers were, yes, I was asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I now want to ask you the following: Is it true and correct that you said on that occasion that as to figures the figures bear out the reliability of the sources and that they go from top to bottom levels of reliability, from 1 to 6? So 1 was least reliable and 6 was the most reliable source.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have on e-court the following document: It is Prosecution Exhibit 503744. P. It is a P document. P 0. P 03744. Now, in the Croatian version it is on page 5, and in English it is on page 6. And in the Spanish version it is on page 2. I think we have everything now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to clear something up. This is why I wanted to have a look at the document. I was talking about reliability in relation to numbers. No reliability [Realtime transcript read in error, "liability"] is given by letters and credibility by the numbers. Reliability, the source; credibility, the news item.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I asked about, figures. I did not inquire whether the document was under seal. I do apologise. So I'm asking now. Is perhaps the document under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is under seal. So we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, and we still have a little time left. Would the Prosecution like to ask any additional questions? If we had exhausted all our time, I wouldn't have asked them that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, have about three questions since we do have the time, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it was mentioned yesterday in connection with the humanitarian convoy, I believe it was the first convoy as we referred to them of the two in August, that when the convoy stopped in Citluk, apart from Mr. Praljak there were a number of other officials or officers there and I believe it was identified that a Foreign Minister of Croatia, Mate Granic, was in Citluk at the time that the convoy was attempting to pass through. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you talk about the second convoy, the one on the 25th of August, because the other one was not in fact stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I stand corrected. Did you have any information, since you were the operational commander of the convoy itself overall, did you have any information that day why the Foreign Minister of the Republic of Croatia, a foreign country, just happened to be in Citluk at the same time that this convoy was passing through?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour, just for the sake of objecting in that he's going beyond the scope of the cross-examination. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a question that could have been asked on direct examination. He failed to do so. So for technical reasons I'm objecting. I don't have a problem with the gentleman answering the question, but I just want to make sure we don't develop a habit of just redoing redirect -- redirect becomes a way to introduce new additional evidence that goes beyond the scope of cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to take up the question, because yesterday it was a question that I asked myself and I wasn't able to ask because of the lack of time. Now, apparently there was somebody who had belonged to another country who was there on the location. That might be surprising, but did you know about this, or what did you learn about the presence of an important person from an important country who was on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no news that the Croatian Foreign Minister was going to be at that time in Citluk, but it was usual for these people to be around, so I was not surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you say it's normal. What's normal, usual? What's usual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Relatively normal for a Croat minister to travel to Mostar, Citluk, to visit refugees, to see the Bosnia-Herzegovina Croatian area for themselves. On a number of occasions we learned of the presence of ministers in the area. I cannot say how many times, but we did learn of their presence in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So what you're telling us is that to your knowledge there were other ministers who visited. Were there any ministers from any other country apart from this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aside from the ones that visited, the Spanish ministers visiting the Spanish forces, we knew of no other ministers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can follow up on the president's questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall knowing or were you briefed at these morning briefings or were you otherwise advised during this time following this extended period of blockade of the eastern -- of the Muslim part of Mostar, were you aware that there was a tremendous international outcry and pressure --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection to the question, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm objecting to the form of the question. It is leading in nature at this point in time. He may ask him an open-ended question as he must and as he should and as he knows. This is direct examination or re-direct. It is not cross-examination. He should not be leading the witness with suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but they are additional questions. Any way, Mr. Scott, you are not cross-examining now. You can't say -- you can't put something to the witness and then say whether -- ask him whether he thinks you're correct. Your questions must be directly linked to what emerged from the cross-examination. So I don't see where you're heading at the moment. Perhaps you could rephrase your question following those guidelines and procedure, the classical procedure. But don't ask him whether he agrees with you. He's not here to agree or not. He's here to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question was not whether he agreed but whether he had been briefed. The witness has advised us that there was a morning briefing every time -- every day, excuse me, that there were reports that were shared amongst all the SpaBat command staff. It may have been that when a senior official of a foreign government was expected to be in the area that day or the following day that that would have been something discussed among the SpaBat command. I'm simply asking if he recalls having any more information about why Mr. Granic, Minister Granic, was there at that time and what the circumstances were in connection with the international position or outcry at that time. If he was advised. If he says he was not advised of that, then we're at an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I need to point this out for the record because this is a sleazy tactic and I'm purposely choosing that word, "sleazy," because he's talking about the outcry. He could have asked the gentleman, what was the briefing about. That was his question. The last part is a sleazy tactic use commonly in the United States by Prosecutors and Defence lawyers when they want to sneak something in front of the jury and I think this is outrageous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But your comments are outrageous, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to deal with the problem. We have a Foreign Minister who was present. The question that the Prosecution was asking, perhaps inappropriately put, which gave rise to the response of the Defence counsel, but when you had meetings, briefings, or meetings amongst yourselves, and this is directly linked to what was said a moment ago about reliability, credibility, did you internally among officers take note of the visit by a foreign person when this convoy was moving? So that's the question. You can say, "I don't remember. We didn't -- we didn't make note of that," or not, well, depending on your answer. Give us your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was -- information was not mentioned at any meeting. There was no mention of a visit by a Foreign Minister nor that I was going to be around the convoy. It was just that whilst we were escorting the convoy he appeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There we have it, the answer, when Mr. Granic was there. Another question, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked today a question about -- you were asked today a question about the fighting around Doljani in April -- mid-April of 1993 and whether Doljani was an area -- a village that was predominantly Croat, was primarily Croat population. All that was put to you by Defence counsel. Did you have any awareness, sir, that the Croat of Doljani had been -- had left the area prior to the attack on the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we knew that there had been population movements. We don't know whether Croats had left Doljani, but there had been movement of population around the whole area because there were combats all around, but I cannot remember, well, the whole of the population, part of the population that left Doljani or not. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Sir, that brings your testimony to a close. I thank you for having come, asked by the Prosecution, called by the Prosecution. You have answered to all our questions, including those of the Judges. We wish you a happy return back home. Before you leave the courtroom may we have the blinds lowered, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to raise the blinds now. Well, if the president could press the button, we'd gain time. Since we have a little time left, there's a problem to resolve, and that is the tendering of documents. I'm going to give the floor to both sides and then -- but, Mr. Scott, as far as the Prosecution documents are concerned, which would you like to have tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Subject to the confirmation because we've just now done this fairly quickly, but subject to further confirmation the specific documents that were put to this witness we believe were the following: In court Exhibit, that is IC 00024, IC 00025, P 01717, P 02081, P 02108, P 02192, P 02220, P 02235, P 02241, P 02273, P 03018, P 03597, P 03705, P 03744, P 03980, P 04423, P 04698, P 09612, apparently that is related to the in court Exhibit 00025, which I already mentioned, and then P 09613, P 093615, P 09676. I would come back to the larger collection of SpaBat documents after we've first dealt with these specific documents, if that's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, what about the Defence, who is going to start off? Counsel Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence of Mr. Pusic presented a number of documents during the cross-examination. The first that we'd like tendered is 6D 0003. Then we have 21 -- 00218, P, was also presented, but since the proposal [as interpreted] tendered the document as a Prosecution document, then we agree. As far as 2291, document 2291 is concerned, it is P 02291, a Prosecution document that we discussed, our proposal was that the document be translate the into English again and then to make the decision of whether to admit it into the evidence or not. And I spoke about this yesterday. Now, another document we used was P 05220. This was not tendered by the Prosecutor just now so we would like to tender it into evidence as a Defence exhibit, but once it's in e-court. We didn't put it into e-court so as not to repeat something that the Prosecutor had perhaps already done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Counsel Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm also going to propose Defence exhibits shown to the witness yesterday. The first exhibit is 2D 0017, and I'd just like to remind the Court that it was information provided by Ivica Lucic. The date is the 14th of June, 1993. In addition to that, I'd like to tender Exhibit 2D 0016, and that is a letter by Mr. Bruno Stojic to the Defence Minister of Spain. Then I'd like to tender Exhibit 2D 0018. I apologise. It is 2D 00118. It is a document, a letter on the civilian police dated the 13th of July, 1993. And finally defence Exhibit 2D 00115, which is a letter from UNPROFOR Malaga, expressing gratitude. I also used yesterday four exhibits; I'll give the numbers: P 0511, P 02741, and P 02761, and just a moment let me check. P 01717. I'll just check that out to see Mr. This as a document included by the Prosecution. If not, we will place it in e-court and then determine a number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. For Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of the accused General Praljak would like to propose the following documents to tender them into evidence: 3D 00278, 3D 00279, 3D 00280, 3D 00310, 3D 00363, 2 -- 3D 00366, it is composed of two parts, a DVD and the transcript, the transcription of the -- of the speakers, 3D 00369 is the next one, 3D 00365, 3D 00340, next two documents, two maps in fact that were used and we were given a provisional number IC 00-0030, and the next document is IC 00-0031, and then just like my colleague, Mrs. Senka, said we would like to put forward the following Prosecution documents I also consider -- I am also one of those who consider that there is no need for a Defence number. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic next.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would like to tender just one document into evidence regardless of the fact that we showed the witness a number of documents and that document is 4D 00070. Now, if I'm wrong on that score I apologise in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just make a correction my colleagues have told me that in the transcript the first document was not recorded that I -- the Prosecution document that I don't think was shown the witness it was P 02108. P 02108. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that my colleague Ms. Alaburic made a mistake I presented that document to the witness not Mr. Scott. So it is not 6D 003, so 0033 at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, but Mr. Scott, it would appear that P 09612 wasn't presented to the witness and you have asked that it be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, our review of the transcript shows that it was used in the transcript on the 22nd of June. We stand by -- let me just clarify because of the various comments of that been made. We stand by the list that I first read to you including that particular document 09612. I did omit one document and that was Exhibit P 03545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the last member of the Defence teams. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I only wish to say that we have no documents to tender through this witness thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I would wish to make a correction. Instead of number 2D 00116, it says 0016 [as interpreted]. So I wish to correct that. I also wish to express my disagreement with the tendering of Prosecution document P 3545. It is a document referring to Mr. Bruno Stojic, but the witness was unable to confirm the content. It concerns a dinner where the witness says he was not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will render a decision concerning all of these documents so we have a few more minutes left. As I see that Mr. Karnavas is here, I would like him to explain to us what he was explaining to us the other day because the Judges failed to understand anything. So could you give us an explanation. I believe that you were requesting the Chamber's assistance, but in order to be provided with assistance, it's nevertheless necessary to be familiar with your objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. I agree, Your Honours. It has to do with the fact that all parties are required to exercise due diligence throughout the course of the trial in order to make a record, so later on if there is an appeal, at least they can -- the Appeals Chamber will be able to see that counsel were due diligent. Now, there is one particular rule, It's 90(H)(i), which is based on a common law principle found in the United Kingdom and other jurisdictions that follow the UK system - unlike the United States - commonly known as putting the case to the witness, and so it requires the Defence, and Mr. Scott on a couple of occasions has indicated that one of us had to put the case to the witness based on this particular Rule. So it requires us to confront the witness with a particular set of questions or documents in order to give the witness an opportunity to give an explanation. I pointed out a document. I used an example yesterday from the direct examination by Mr. Scott where he was looking at -- he had -- there was a series of questions, and throughout his direct examination he had made references to a particular operational logbook. The one set of questions was related to why were the Muslims -- why did they blockade the SpaBat in Mostar? Why didn't they let them leave, the convoy. And so the answer that was given was -- and I pointed for the record the relevant pages, but the answer was they wanted to give the UN a taste of what it was like to be under siege in essence. In the very same document that was being referenced by Mr. Scott for other purposes, there was an entry for, I believe it was August 31st, wherein it said that the reasons that they believed that they were blockade -- that there was the blockade was because they wanted the time to regroup in order to, at some point, to have some sort of a tactical advantage obviously they were getting ready for an attack. There was a clear instance where the Prosecution in my opinion should have presented this to the Trial Chamber. They did not. It's an adversarial setting. I understand that. But one would -- could argue that there should be some sort of an affirmative duty on the part of the Prosecutor or the other side as well to point out those flaws, but more so on the Prosecution because, after all, we have no burden of proof. Be that as it may, I chose not to cross-examine on that issue for a variety of reasons and one was to make this particular point and see if I'm correct. Since the gentleman did not generate the document himself, I felt that there was no need for me to confront the witness and take up time since I would nonetheless be able to use that portion of the document in future purposes such as in the final brief to show that there's another alternative plausible explanation and therefore there was no need for me to confront the witness. And so -- the way I understand the Rule is, and I think the way perhaps the Trial Chamber may wish to give us some guidance on, that we need only put the case to the witness where the document that is being referenced, for instance, is one that was generated by the witness himself. Of course, we would be -- we would feel free to so confront the witness, but we would not be exercising lack of diligence for failing to confront a witness with a document not generated by that particular witness but for the sheer sake of showing a contradiction, and that's where I thought that the Trial Chamber may wish to consider and give us some guidance. Now, I mentioned this because, if the answer is no, you must put the case to the witness, then it will take up a tremendous amount of time for the Defence during the cross-examination period, and under the time constraints and the realities that exist, we simply don't have that time. And I don't think anyone is prejudiced because the documents are there, and I would say this is more of a continental approach than one might -- than one, say, I would exercise in my own jurisdiction, especially in front of a jury, keeping in mind that we don't have a final brief in front of a jury. That's one point. I hope I've clarified that or perhaps, if there are any questions on that. I would like to move on to another issue again dealing with how we may be able to find ways to get around the time constraints that would allow both parties and the Trial Chamber to -- to have a fair trial in this -- in this setting. And -- and I would ask the Trial Chamber to perhaps entertain, under Rule 71, it provides for depositions, and I think if we look at the other Rules, obviously the Trial Chamber is free to exercise its discretion. It has a wide degree of discretion. And here is how Rule 71 may be of assistance. Tomljanovich, from what I understand this morning the ruling was that essentially each Defence team, each accused gets two hours to cross-examine Mr. Tomljanovich, approximately. Give or take a minute here or there. Clearly that is not enough, particularly if the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You are making a mistake. This morning we said in total the Defence has three days. It's for you to decide how to allocate this time. If you decide that Mr. Prlic's Defence will have all that time, the Chamber agrees but if you fail to reach an agreement, in that case, the Bench will have to rule. And naturally we would prefer you to reach an agreement the bench would prefer you to reach an agreement amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I said essentially, Your Honour. I mean if we divide it I'm not suggesting that -- I understand it was three days, but we cannot always agree as you well have noticed by now but be that as it may, 12 hours. Now, the Prosecution has indicated that they want to bring in portions of the report and -- and of course -- direct examine him as well. And in doing that, obviously it puts the Defence in a very difficult position because we would need more time, substantially more than what is being provided. I understand the problems that we have, but one way to get around it perhaps might be to schedule a deposition of Mr. Tomljanovich, say on Friday. And we can do this with a court officers and it won't take up any time of the Judges and during the deposition at least we could cover a great deal of the preliminary issues. It would be under oath. You would have the record. Objections could be raised. So -- and then when we come into court we would have a much more useful -- we would use the time more usefully by getting directly into the issue. I throw that out as one example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise for interrupting you, but this witness is considered to be an expert witness. He shouldn't shall heard in the way that you have suggested. He's and expert witness even if he's being paid for his testimony. That's the case for the Prosecution. Your idea is very interesting, but he is the Prosecution's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in any case, the witness will take the solemn declaration before his testimony. He'll answer your questions, the Judges's questions, the Prosecution's questions, after taking the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here's the problem I'm confronted with, Your Honour if, if I may use a culinary example. Anybody who knows about cooking knows there is a certain procedure that needs to be followed and I'm constantly being told, go directly, go directly, go directly, why are you doing this? Why is it necessary to talk about that? Why? Because I need to lay a foundation; I need to lock the witness in; I need to lay the groundwork. It's not just by coincidence. Hundreds of hours are spent preparing for cross-examination, and I dare say they're wasted. They're wasted because we don't have the time. The man is an expert, if you want to call him that. I choose not to. I don't think he is an expert. He's a historian but he's not a political scientist. But what I'm suggesting Your Honour is not technical questions with relation to his expertise but rather the background. For instance, I would like to know what his salary is, I want to know what he has earned with the UN, I want to know what his package is I want to know which -- you know, all these sorts of things that would take up a lot of my time that you would not want me to take up, that time here in court, and want me to get directly into the heart of the matter. I'm merely suggesting this we don't have to do it with Mr. Tomljanovich. I have another idea as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you very well, but to ask him how much he earns, how can that help? Why would that be relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How would that affect the technical aspects of his report unless one suggests that he is being well paid because he has drafted a report of a certain kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was a fine example by Mr. Kovacic. Why not have Ms. Nika Pinter who has been here in these cases more than anyone else in this courtroom, why not have her testify as an expert witness on behalf of General Praljak? She's an expert. That's what we're talking about. We're talking about an employee, a member of the team, somebody who gets paid. Now, is he going to disagree with his pay masters? He gets fired. The reason he keeps his job is he's part of the team. He's participating --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's pure assertion by Mr. Karnavas. That's slander of a human being that's in this courtroom to defend himself without any basis to do so. He's said that he's put himself up for hire. Now that's an allegation that is unfounded and it's outrageous for Mr. Karnavas to make it. He should stop making allegations that he cannot support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's part of a team. He sits in -- he sits in strategy sessions he interviews witnesses he goes into the field. And I can go on down the list. He is no different than having Mr. Mundis in court. Why not have him testify on behalf of the Prosecution as an expert witness? That's what we're talking about. There's no difference. He lacks a law degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've taken note of what you have said. The Judges will discuss the matter. You have raised an issue that shocked me personally when I first arrived in this Tribunal, but Judges in other Trial Chambers have accepted such a procedure. As you're a member of the Defence association, you can ask the Rules committee or you can submit a motion to the Rules committee to have certain Rules amended, and believe me I will fully support you. Unfortunately, I have to declare the session adjourned because there is another trial in the afternoon. Tomorrow the Prosecution will need two hours for our next witness and as the victim is concerned the Defence will also have two hours. It's for you to decide how to divide this time. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you up because we are leaving or is there something you would like to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour there are two things one I absolutely have to do because -- well, I can take it up with the registry about the protective measures requested by the witness for tomorrow. I'll take it up with the registry directly. Ten seconds, Your Honour. Before the Court makes any rulings on the matters this afternoon I want to be -- with all respect, I want to be heard on them. Mr. Karnavas has got on his feet for an extended period of time and raised a number issues from A to Z. I've had no opportunity to respond to them whatsoever there was another issue raised about another exhibit I had no chance to respond to I also said I wanted to object -- to raise the whole issue of the documents generally and, Your Honour, with all respect I want to have the appropriate time to address the matters that are important to the Prosecution as well so I will ask to have time tomorrow to do that as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. Tomorrow you will need two hours for the witness. Or perhaps you could shorten your examination and than would give you more time for your intervention. Thank you. And I will see everyone tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 31st day of August, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
